newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania president greets death-row nationalist.
newsitem.headline: Romania president greets death-row nationalist.

text.p: Romanian President Emil Constantinescu sent birthday greetings on Thursday to an ethnic Romanian nationalist facing a death sentence in neighbouring Moldova's separatist Dnestr region.
A message issued by Constantinescu's press office on Ilie Ilascu's 45th birthday also said efforts to win his release were backed by the leaders of ex-Soviet Ukraine and Moldova.
He hoped to win similar assurances from Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
"I assure you that your situation, dramatic and laden with special emotion for us Romanians, is one of my constant and main preoccupations," Constantinescu said.

The president regretted that Dnestr's Russian-speaking separatist leaders, who fought troops from newly-independent Moldova in 1992, had barred him from visiting Ilascu during his presidential campaign last year.

But he said Moldovan President Petru Lucinschi and Ukrainian leader Leonid Kuchma had assured him in recent talks of "the special interest which they devote to your case. I hope that our wish will find a favourable response too, with President Yeltsin."
Yeltsin has made no public statements on Ilascu's fate.

Ilascu, a proponent of reuniting Moldova with Romania, was sentenced to death in 1993 on terrorism charges by a court in the Dnestr region, which has no international recognition. He was elected a member of Moldova's parliament a year later.

Five other defendants were sentenced to prison terms in connection with 1992 fighting pitting Moldovan troops against Dnestr rebel forces, halted after intervention by Russia's 14th army. One has since been released.
Most of independent Moldova was part of Romania between the world wars but was seized by the Kremlin in 1940 under the Nazi-Soviet pact dividing up eastern Europe.

Dnestr's hardline communist leaders proclaimed independence in 1990, before the collapse of the Soviet Union, fearing that they would become second-class citizens if Moldova's ethnic Romanian majority opted to rejoin Romania.
Calls for reunification after the fall of communism are now confined to a tiny minority on both sides of the border.
Moldovan and Dnestr leaders signed a peace accord in May, brokered by Ukraine and Russia.
But Dnestr leaders insist the region is a separate entity. An earlier agreement to withdraw Russian troops from the region is still awaiting ratification by Moscow's communist-dominated parliament.
